name: Availability Bias
description: Judging the probability or importance of events by how easily examples come to mind, rather than by actual base rates.
detectionHints: vivid recent examples presented as typical
anecdote treated as evidence of frequency
emotional story used to imply scale
lack of denominator or base rate
what comes to mind easily must be common
examples: After one plane crash is heavily covered, people overestimate the danger of flying.
A single dramatic crime story used to claim a city is collapsing.
counterMeasures: Ask for base rates and denominators.
Seek statistical data instead of vivid cases.
Check how representative the example actually is.
historicalAnalogs: Post-9/11 overestimation of terrorism risk relative to other causes of death.
Media-driven moral panics throughout the 20th century.

name: Missing Denominator
description: Presenting absolute numbers without the relevant base rate or population size, making the figure appear more alarming or impressive than it is.
detectionHints: large absolute number with no rate
percentage increase without original baseline
raw count presented as crisis
out of how many is never stated
examples: "10,000 people died from X last year" without mentioning the population or comparison to other causes.
counterMeasures: Always ask: out of how many?
Request rates per 100,000 or per capita.
Compare to historical or peer baselines.

name: Moral Framing
description: Casting an issue primarily in terms of good vs evil or virtue vs vice to short-circuit trade-off thinking and evidence evaluation.
detectionHints: language of pure good and pure evil
opponents described as immoral rather than mistaken
complex policy reduced to a moral test
on the right side of history
compassion versus cruelty framing
examples: Any disagreement framed as being 'on the wrong side of history'.
Policy debate turned into a referendum on compassion.
counterMeasures: Separate the moral claim from the empirical claim.
Ask what trade-offs exist.
Request evidence independent of the moral narrative.
historicalAnalogs: Many religious and political movements across history.

name: False Dichotomy
description: Presenting only two options when more exist, forcing a choice between extremes.
detectionHints: either X or Y framing
absence of middle positions or alternatives
forced binary in a complex space
you are either with us or against us
examples: "You are either with us or against us."
Policy debates reduced to two caricatured camps.
counterMeasures: Explicitly list additional options.
Ask what is being left out of the frame.
Refuse the binary.

name: Confirmation Bias
description: Seeking, interpreting, and remembering information in a way that confirms preexisting beliefs while discounting contradictory evidence.
detectionHints: only sources that agree are cited
contradictory data dismissed as biased
selective memory of hits and misses
searching for evidence of rather than evidence against
examples: Reading only media that shares one's political views.
Remembering the times a superstition worked and forgetting the times it did not.
counterMeasures: Actively seek the strongest opposing evidence.
Ask: what would change my mind?
Keep a record of predictions and outcomes.

name: Fear Appeal
description: Using threats of harm or vivid negative consequences to motivate compliance or belief, often without proportional evidence.
detectionHints: vivid catastrophic scenarios
if we don't act now something terrible will happen
emotional threat outweighing evidence
urgency + danger pairing
examples: Advertisements that show extreme outcomes from not using a product.
Political messaging that paints opponents as existential threats.
counterMeasures: Separate the emotional intensity from the actual probability and magnitude.
Ask for base rates of the feared outcome.
Check whether the recommended action actually reduces the risk.

name: Loaded Language
description: Using words with strong emotional connotations to influence judgment without providing additional evidence.
detectionHints: emotionally charged adjectives and nouns
words that smuggle in evaluations
labeling instead of describing
euphemism or dysphemism replacing neutral terms
examples: Calling a policy radical or common-sense instead of describing its content.
Referring to people with loaded labels instead of neutral terms.
counterMeasures: Replace loaded terms with neutral descriptions.
Ask what concrete claim remains after the emotional words are removed.
Notice when language is doing the work of argument.

name: Social Proof / Bandwagon
description: Treating the popularity or widespread acceptance of a claim or behavior as evidence of its correctness or desirability.
detectionHints: everyone is doing it
millions of users can't be wrong
most people believe
join the movement language
examples: Join the millions who already switched.
Citing majority opinion as proof of truth.
counterMeasures: Popularity is not evidence of truth or quality.
Ask for independent reasons why the claim is true.
Majorities have been wrong many times.
